Analytic properties arising from the Baxter numbers

Hanqian Fang Note: KLMM, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, P.R. China. Email: fanghanqian22@mails.ucas.ac.cn.    Candice X.T. Zhang Note: KLMM, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, P.R. China. Email: zhangxutong@amss.ac.cn.    James J.Y. Zhao Note: School of Accounting, Guangzhou College of Technology and Business, Foshan 528138, P.R. China. Email: zhao@gzgs.edu.cn.
Abstract

Baxter numbers are known as the enumeration of Baxter permutations and numerous other discrete structures, playing a significant role across combinatorics, algebra, and analysis. In this paper, we focus on the analytic properties related to Baxter numbers. We prove that the descent polynomials of Baxter permutations have interlacing zeros, which is a property stronger than real-rootedness. Our approach is based on Dilks’ framework of (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sums, which is a qq-analog for Baxter permutations. Within this framework, we show that the family of (1,t)(1,t)-Hoggatt sums satisfies the interlacing property using fundamental results on Hadamard products of polynomials. For Baxter numbers, we prove their asymptotic rr-log-convexity via asymptotic expansions of PP-recursive sequences. In particular, we confirm their 22-log-convexity using symbolic computation techniques.

AMS Classification 2020: 26C10; 11B83; 05A10

Keywords: Baxter number; Hoggatt sum; Sturm sequence; asymptotic rr-log-convexity; Hadamard product

1 Introduction

The Baxter permutations were first introduced by Glen Baxter [1] in 1964 in the context of studying the fixed points of the composition of commuting functions. A Baxter permutation on [n][n] is a permutation π=π1π2⋯πn∈𝔖n\pi=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\cdots\pi_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} which avoids all subsequences πi​πj​πj+1​πk\pi_{i}\pi_{j}\pi_{j+1}\pi_{k} (for indices i<j<k−1i<j<k-1) satisfying either of the following patterns:

πj+1<πi<πk<πj or πj<πk<πi<πj+1.\pi_{j+1}<\pi_{i}<\pi_{k}<\pi_{j}\quad\text{ or }\quad\pi_{j}<\pi_{k}<\pi_{i}<\pi_{j+1}.

These permutations have significance in combinatorics, algebra and analysis. Various bijections have been built between Baxter permutations and other combinatorial objects, such as twisted Baxter permutations [18], pairs of twin binary trees on nn nodes [15], plane partitions in a box [8], and so on. These objects form the well-known “Baxter family”. In addition, it turns out that these objects possess elegant algebraic properties and thus become suitable candidates to index the bases of some Hopf algebras. For more details, see [24, 18, 6]. From an analytic perspective, inspired by the bijection between Baxter permutations and plane partitions in a box, Dilks [9] gave a natural qq-analog for Baxter permutations, called the (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sums, and further proved their qq-gamma nonnegativity. From a matrix perspective, Mao and Shi [22] studied various properties on log-behaviors in the mm-Hoggatt triangle, whose row generating functions are the (1,t)(1,t)-Hoggatt sums. Furthermore, they also obtained the asymptotic normality of the row sequences and total positivity of the mm-Hoggatt triangle. In this paper, we delve deeper into the analytic properties arising from the Baxter permutations.

Baxter permutations are counted by Baxter numbers BnB_{n} [25, A001181] with the formula

Bn=∑k=1n2n​(n+1)2​(n+1k−1)​(n+1k)​(n+1k+1).B_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{2}{n(n+1)^{2}}\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1}. (1.1)

This formula was first established by Chung et al. [7] with analytical methods, and later by Viennot [27] through combinatorial bijections. The sum terms in Equation (1.1), defined as

Dn,k=2n​(n+1)2​(n+1k−1)​(n+1k)​(n+1k+1),D_{n,\,k}=\frac{2}{n(n+1)^{2}}\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1},

also have corresponding combinatorial interpretations within the Baxter family. Mallows [20] first showed that Dn,kD_{n,\,k} counts the reduced Baxter permutations on [n][n] with exactly kk rises. Felsner et al. further presented a unifying presentation for the bijections between the objects in Baxter family, which implies that Dn,kD_{n,\,k} also counts the Baxter permutations on [n][n] with k−1k-1 descents and n−kn-k rises [12, Proposition 6.8], twin pairs of binary trees with kk left leaves and n−k+1n-k+1 right leaves [12, Theorem 5.6], and so on. These results demonstrate that the study of the numbers Dn,kD_{n,\,k} is not only intriguing in its own right, but also crucial for understanding Baxter numbers BnB_{n}. Therefore, we define the Baxter polynomial P​Bn​(t)PB_{n}(t) to be the generating function of Dn,kD_{n,\,k}, i.e.,

P​Bn​(t):=∑k=1nDn,k​tk−1=∑k=1n2n​(n+1)2​(n+1k−1)​(n+1k)​(n+1k+1)​tk−1PB_{n}(t):=\sum_{k=1}^{n}D_{n,\,k}t^{k-1}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{2}{n(n+1)^{2}}\binom{n+1}{k-1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n+1}{k+1}t^{k-1}

for n≥1n\geq 1. Note that P​Bn​(t)PB_{n}(t) can be equivalently interpreted as the descent polynomials of Baxter permutations.

As stated above, Dilks [9] placed Baxter polynomials within a broader framework of the (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sums, defined by

Hn[m]​(q,t)=∑k+l=n−1M⁡(k,l,m,q)​tk,\displaystyle H_{n}^{[m]}(q,t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+l=n-1\end{subarray}}M(k,l,m;q)t^{k},

where

M⁡(k,l,m,q)=qm​(k+12)​∑π∈PPk,l,mq|π|,\displaystyle M(k,l,m;q)=q^{m\binom{k+1}{2}}\sum_{\pi\in\textrm{PP}_{k,\,l,\,m}}q^{|\pi|},

and PPk,l,m\textrm{PP}_{k,\,l,\,m} denotes the set of all plane partitions in a k×l×mk\times l\times m box. These polynomials are the qq-analogs of the Hoggatt sums, originally introduced by Fielder and Alford [13] in the study of Hoggatt’s conjecture related to Pascal’s triangle and Baxter permutations. For the special case q=1q=1, the (1,t)(1,t)-Hoggatt sum reduces to

Hn[m]​(1,t)=∑k=0n−1∏i=0m−1(n+m−2k+i)∏j=1m−1(n+m−2j)​tk,\displaystyle H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\binom{n+m-2}{k+i}}{\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\binom{n+m-2}{j}}t^{k},

where the coefficient counts the number of plane partitions fitting in a k×(n−1−k)×mk\times(n-1-k)\times m box, see [26, Theorem 7.21.7]. Notably, when m=3m=3, the polynomial Hn[m]​(1,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t) specializes to the Baxter polynomial P​Bn​(t)PB_{n}(t). In the remainder of this paper, we call the (1,t)(1,t)-Hoggatt sums Hn[m]​(1,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t) the Hoggatt polynomials.

For all m≥1m\geq 1, the real-rootedness of the Hoggatt polynomials Hn[m]​(1,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t) has been obtained by Dilks [9, Theorem 3.8] via the theory of multiplier sequences [3]. Motivated by this, one of the main objectives of this paper is to explore the interlacing property of the polynomial sequence {Hn[m]​(1,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)\}_{n\geq 1} for any fixed m≥1m\geq 1.

For the purpose of describing our main theorem, we need the following definitions and notations. Given two real-rooted polynomials f⁡(t)f(t), g⁡(t)g(t) with real coefficients, let {ui}\{u_{i}\} and {vj}\{v_{j}\} be all zeros of f⁡(t)f(t) and g⁡(t)g(t) in weakly decreasing order, respectively. We say that g⁡(t)g(t) interlaces f⁡(t)f(t) if deg⁡f⁡(t)=deg⁡g⁡(t)+1=n\deg f(t)=\deg g(t)+1=n and

un≤vn−1≤un−1≤⋯≤v2≤u2≤v1≤u1.\displaystyle{u_{n}\leq v_{n-1}\leq u_{n-1}\leq\cdots\leq v_{2}\leq u_{2}\leq v_{1}\leq u_{1}}. (1.2)

We say that g⁡(t)g(t) alternates left of f⁡(t)f(t) if deg⁡f⁡(t)=deg⁡g⁡(t)=n\deg f(t)=\deg g(t)=n and

vn≤un≤vn−1≤un−1≤⋯≤v2≤u2≤v1≤u1.\displaystyle{v_{n}\leq u_{n}\leq v_{n-1}\leq u_{n-1}\leq\cdots\leq v_{2}\leq u_{2}\leq v_{1}\leq u_{1}}. (1.3)

Denote by g⁡(t)⪯f⁡(t)g(t)\preceq f(t) if either g⁡(t)g(t) interlaces f⁡(t)f(t) or g⁡(t)g(t) alternates left of f⁡(t)f(t). We say that g⁡(t)g(t) strictly interlaces (resp., strictly alternates left of) f⁡(t)f(t) if no equality holds in (1.2) (resp., (1.3)). Write g⁡(t)≺f⁡(t)g(t)\prec f(t) if g⁡(t)g(t) strictly interlaces or strictly alternates left of f⁡(t)f(t). For convenience, we also let a⪯b​x+ca\preceq bx+c for any nonnegative real numbers a,b,ca,b,c, and f⁡(t)⪯0f(t)\preceq 0, 0⪯f⁡(t)0\preceq f(t) for any real polynomial f⁡(t)f(t) with only real zeros. A sequence of real-rooted polynomials {fn​(t)}n≥0\{f_{n}(t)\}_{n\geq 0} is said to be a Sturm sequence if

f0​(t)≺f1​(t)≺⋯≺fn​(t)≺⋯,{f_{0}(t)\prec f_{1}(t)\prec\cdots\prec f_{n}(t)\prec\cdots},

and it is said to be a generalized Sturm sequence if

f0​(t)⪯f1​(t)⪯⋯⪯fn​(t)⪯⋯.{f_{0}(t)\preceq f_{1}(t)\preceq\cdots\preceq f_{n}(t)\preceq\cdots}.

We can now give our main results as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

The sequence of Baxter polynomials {P​Bn​(t)}n≥1\{PB_{n}(t)\}_{n\geq 1} is a Sturm sequence.

In fact, we obtain a more general result in the framework of Hoggatt polynomial sequence {Hn[m]​(1,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)\}_{n\geq 1} by induction on mm.

Theorem 1.2.

For m=1m=1, the sequence of Hoggatt polynomials {Hn[1]​(1,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[1]}(1,t)\}_{n\geq 1} is a generalized Sturm sequence. For any integer m≥2m\geq 2, the sequence {Hn[m]​(1,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)\}_{n\geq 1} is a Sturm sequence.

Since a (generalized) Sturm sequence must be a real-rooted polynomial sequence, we also provide an alternative proof for the real-rootedness result established by Dilks [9, Theorem 3.8]. Note that the coefficients of a real-rooted polynomial sequence are usually asymptotically normal. For instance, the asymptotic normality of the numbers Dn,kD_{n,\,k} was obtained by Zhao [32]. Recently, Mao and Shi [22] extended this result to the coefficients M⁡(k,n−k−1,m,1)M(k,n-k-1,m;1) of Hoggatt polynomials. In addition, the real-rootedness of a polynomial also implies the log-concavity of its coefficient sequence via the well-known Newton inequality. Furthermore, if this polynomial has only negative zeros, Brändén [4] showed that its coefficient sequence is infinitely log-concave, a stronger definition introduced by Boros and Moll [5]. Utilizing this result, Mao and Shi [22, Theorem 2.3] remarked that the sequence {M⁡(k,n−k−1,m,1)}k=0n−1\{M(k,n-k-1,m;1)\}_{k=0}^{n-1} is infinitely log-concave for any integers n≥1n\geq 1 and m≥1m\geq 1. As a special case, this implies the infinite log-concavity of the sequence {Dn,k}k=1n\{D_{n,\,k}\}_{k=1}^{n}.

Our second main result focuses on the log-convexity property, a dual notion of log-concavity, of the Baxter numbers BnB_{n}. Recall that an infinite sequence {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is said to be log-convex if an2≤an−1​an+1a_{n}^{2}\leq a_{n-1}a_{n+1} for n≥1n\geq 1. Let ℒ\mathscr{L} be the operator defined by

ℒ⁡({an}n≥0)={an​an+2−an+12}n≥0.\mathscr{L}\left(\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\right)=\{a_{n}a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}^{2}\}_{n\geq 0}.

A sequence {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is said to be rr-log-convex if the jj-th iterative sequence ℒj​({an}n≥0)\mathscr{L}^{j}\left(\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\right) is nonnegative for all 1≤j≤r1\leq j\leq r. Furthermore, {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is said to be infinitely log-convex if it is rr-log-convex for all r≥1r\geq 1. Hou and Zhang [16] introduced the concept of asymptotic rr-log-convexity of {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} which requires that for each 1≤j≤r1\leq j\leq r, the sequence ℒj​({an}n≥0)\mathscr{L}^{j}\left(\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\right) is nonnegative for all but finitely many initial terms. The log-convexity of the Baxter number sequence {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} was obtained in [11, Theorem 4.18] by Došlić and Veljan. In this paper, we focus on the (asymptotic) rr-log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}.

Theorem 1.3.

The sequence {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is asymptotically rr-log-convex for any integer r≥1r\geq 1. In particular, for r=2r=2, the sequence {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is 22-log-convex.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we prove Theorem 1.2 by applying Garloff and Wagner’s results on Hadamard products of interlacing polynomials and Dimitrov’s work concerning derivatives of interlacing polynomials. Section 3 is devoted to the study of (asymptotic) rr-log-convexity of Baxter numbers. We show a proof of Theorem 1.3 with some tools in asymptotic expansions of PP-recursive sequences given by Hou and Zhang. In Section 4, we conclude this paper by proposing three conjectures related to (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sums and Baxter numbers.

2 Interlacing property of Hoggatt polynomials

The aim of this section is to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2. To this end, we first recall two operations, Hadamard product and polynomial derivative, which preserve the interlacing property.

The Hadamard product of two polynomials f⁡(t)=∑i=0nai​tif(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}a_{i}t^{i} and g⁡(t)=∑i=0mbi​tig(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}b_{i}t^{i} is defined to be

f⁡(t)∗g⁡(t)=∑i=0kai​bi​ti,\displaystyle f(t)*g(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}a_{i}b_{i}t^{i}, (2.1)

where k=min⁡{m,n}k=\min\{m,n\}. Maló [21] first proved that the Hadamard product preserves the real-rootedness of polynomials. Later, Garloff and Wagner [14] extended Maló’s result as follows.

Theorem 2.1 ([14, Theorem 4]).

Let f⁡(t),g⁡(t),p⁡(t),q⁡(t)∈ℝ⁡[t]f(t),\,g(t),\,p(t),\,q(t)\in\mathbb{R}[t] with positive leading coefficients and only nonpositive zeros.

  • (1)

    If f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t)≠0f(t)*p(t)\neq 0, then f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t)f(t)*p(t) has only nonpositive zeros which are simple except possibly at the origin.

  • (2)

    If g⁡(t)⪯f⁡(t)g(t)\preceq f(t) and q⁡(t)⪯p⁡(t)q(t)\preceq p(t), then we have

    g⁡(t)∗q⁡(t)⪯f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t).g(t)*q(t)\preceq f(t)*p(t).
  • (3)

    If g⁡(t)⪯f⁡(t)g(t)\preceq f(t) and q⁡(t)⪯p⁡(t)q(t)\preceq p(t), f⁡(t),g⁡(t),p⁡(t)f(t),\,g(t),\,p(t) and q⁡(t)q(t) are all nonzero, and neither f⁡(t)=c1​g​(t)f(t)=c_{1}g(t) and p⁡(t)=c2​q​(t)p(t)=c_{2}q(t) nor f⁡(t)=c1​t​g​(t)f(t)=c_{1}tg(t) and p⁡(t)=c2​t​q​(t)p(t)=c_{2}tq(t) for any c1,c2>0c_{1},\,c_{2}>0, then we have

    gcd⁡(g⁡(t)∗q⁡(t),f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t))=tr,\displaystyle\gcd(g(t)*q(t),f(t)*p(t))=t^{r}, (2.2)

    where rr is the maximum multiplicity of t=0t=0 as a zero of the polynomials g⁡(t)g(t) and q⁡(t)q(t).

To better demonstrate Theorem 1.2, we simplify the above theorem as the following corollary.

Corollary 2.1.

Let f⁡(t),g⁡(t),p⁡(t),q⁡(t)∈ℝ⁡[t]f(t),\,g(t),\,p(t),\,q(t)\in\mathbb{R}[t] with positive leading coefficients and only negative zeros. If g⁡(t)g(t) interlaces f⁡(t)f(t) and q⁡(t)q(t) interlaces p⁡(t)p(t), then we have

g⁡(t)∗q⁡(t)≺f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t).g(t)*q(t)\prec f(t)*p(t).
Proof.

According to (2) of Theorem 2.1, one can first deduce that

g⁡(t)∗q⁡(t)⪯f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t).\displaystyle g(t)*q(t)\preceq f(t)*p(t). (2.3)

Furthermore, under the given conditions, we have deg⁡f⁡(t)=deg⁡g⁡(t)+1\deg f(t)=\deg g(t)+1, deg⁡p⁡(t)=deg⁡q⁡(t)+1\deg p(t)=\deg q(t)+1, and f⁡(t),g⁡(t),p⁡(t),q⁡(t)f(t),\,g(t),\,p(t),\,q(t) do not vanish at the origin. These imply that f⁡(t)≠c1​g​(t)f(t)\neq c_{1}g(t), p⁡(t)≠c2​q​(t)p(t)\neq c_{2}q(t), f⁡(t)≠c3​t​g​(t)f(t)\neq c_{3}tg(t) and p⁡(t)≠c4​t​q​(t)p(t)\neq c_{4}tq(t) for any c1,c2,c3,c4>0c_{1},\,c_{2},\,c_{3},\,c_{4}>0. Utilizing (3) of Theorem 2.1, we can obtain that r=0r=0 in Equation (2.2) and thus

gcd⁡(g⁡(t)∗q⁡(t),f⁡(t)∗p⁡(t))=tr=1.\gcd(g(t)*q(t),f(t)*p(t))=t^{r}=1.

As a result, the relation (2.3) holds strictly. ∎

Another crucial tool is a celebrated result on polynomial derivative given by Markov [23], which was restated by Dimitrov [10, Page 70].

Theorem 2.2 ([23, §16]).

Let f⁡(t)f(t) and g⁡(t)g(t) be real algebraic polynomials with only real and distinct zeros. If g⁡(t)≺f⁡(t)g(t)\prec f(t), then g′​(t)≺f′​(t)g^{\prime}(t)\prec f^{\prime}(t).

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 1.2, which includes Theorem 1.1 as a special case.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

For convenience, we set

Fn,m(t):=∑k=0n−m+1(nk)(nk+1)⋯(nk+m−1)tk.F_{n,\,m}(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{n-m+1}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k+1}\cdots\binom{n}{k+m-1}t^{k}. (2.4)

This simplifies the expression of Hn[m]​(1,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t) since

Hn[m]​(1,t)=\displaystyle H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)= 1(n+m−21)(n+m−22)⋯(n+m−2m−1)∑k=0n−1(n+m−2k)(n+m−2k+1)⋯(n+m−2k+m−1)tk\displaystyle\,\frac{1}{\binom{n+m-2}{1}\binom{n+m-2}{2}\cdots\binom{n+m-2}{m-1}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{n+m-2}{k}\binom{n+m-2}{k+1}\cdots\binom{n+m-2}{k+m-1}t^{k}
=\displaystyle= 1(n+m−21)(n+m−22)⋯(n+m−2m−1)​Fn+m−2,m​(t).\displaystyle\,\frac{1}{\binom{n+m-2}{1}\binom{n+m-2}{2}\cdots\binom{n+m-2}{m-1}}F_{n+m-2,\,m}(t).

Then the assertion for m=1m=1 is trivial since Hn[1]​(1,t)=Fn−1, 1​(t)=(t+1)n−1H_{n}^{[1]}(1,t)=F_{n-1,\,1}(t)=(t+1)^{n-1} for n≥1n\geq 1. Now it suffices to prove that for any fixed m≥2m\geq 2, the sequence {Fn,m​(t)}n≥m−1\{F_{n,\,m}(t)\}_{n\geq m-1} is a Sturm sequence by induction on m≥2m\geq 2.

For m=2m=2, we have (n+1)​Fn, 2​(t)=(Fn, 1​(t)∗Fn+1, 1​(t))′(n+1)F_{n,\,2}(t)=(F_{n,\,1}(t)*F_{n+1,\,1}(t))^{\prime} by the definitions (2.1) and (2.4). It is evident that Fn−1, 1​(t)F_{n-1,\,1}(t) interlaces Fn, 1​(t)F_{n,\,1}(t) for any n≥2n\geq 2. Thus the sequence {Fn, 2​(t)}n≥1\{F_{n,\,2}(t)\}_{n\geq 1} is a Sturm sequence by Corollary 2.1 and Theorem 2.2.

For m≥2m\geq 2, suppose that {Fn,m−1​(t)}n≥m−2\{F_{n,\,m-1}(t)\}_{n\geq m-2} is a Sturm sequence. We proceed to prove that for any n≥mn\geq m,

Fn−1,m​(t)≺Fn,m​(t).\displaystyle F_{n-1,\,m}(t)\prec F_{n,\,m}(t). (2.5)

To achieve this, we construct an auxiliary polynomial Gn,m​(t)G_{n,\,m}(t) as follows:

Gn,m​(t)\displaystyle G_{n,\,m}(t) =Fn, 1​(t)∗Fn−1,m−1​(t)\displaystyle=F_{n,\,1}(t)*F_{n-1,\,m-1}(t)
=∑k=0n−m+1(nk)⋅((n−1k)(n−1k+1)⋯(n−1k+m−2))⋅tk.\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-m+1}\binom{n}{k}\cdot\left(\binom{n-1}{k}\binom{n-1}{k+1}\cdots\binom{n-1}{k+m-2}\right)\cdot t^{k}.

Since the polynomials Fn, 1​(t)F_{n,\,1}(t) and Fn−1,m−1​(t)F_{n-1,\,m-1}(t) have nonzero constant and their coefficients are all positive, it is clear that they have only negative zeros. Thus the polynomial Gn,m​(t)G_{n,\,m}(t) has only nonpositive zeros by (1) of Theorem 2.1. Besides, we have deg⁡Fn,m​(t)=n−m+1\deg F_{n,\,m}(t)=n-m+1 for any n≥m−1n\geq m-1. Combining the fact that Fn, 1​(t)⪯Fn+1, 1​(t)F_{n,\,1}(t)\preceq F_{n+1,\,1}(t) and the inductive hypothesis

Fn−1,m−1​(t)≺Fn,m−1​(t),\displaystyle F_{n-1,\,m-1}(t)\prec F_{n,\,m-1}(t),

we apply Corollary 2.1 to conclude that

Gn,m​(t)≺Gn+1,m​(t).\displaystyle G_{n,\,m}(t)\prec G_{n+1,\,m}(t).

This implies that

Gn,m′​(t)≺Gn+1,m′​(t)\displaystyle G_{n,\,m}^{\prime}(t)\prec G_{n+1,\,m}^{\prime}(t) (2.6)

by Theorem 2.2. We see that

Gn,m′​(t)\displaystyle G_{n,\,m}^{\prime}(t) =∑k=0n−m+1k(nk)(n−1k)(n−1k+1)⋯(n−1k+m−2)tk−1\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-m+1}k\binom{n}{k}\binom{n-1}{k}\binom{n-1}{k+1}\cdots\binom{n-1}{k+m-2}t^{k-1}
=∑k=0n−m(k+1)(nk+1)(n−1k+1)(n−1k+2)⋯(n−1k+m−1)tk\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-m}(k+1)\binom{n}{k+1}\binom{n-1}{k+1}\binom{n-1}{k+2}\cdots\binom{n-1}{k+m-1}t^{k}
=n∑k=0n−m(n−1k)(n−1k+1)(n−1k+2)⋯(n−1k+m−1)tk\displaystyle=n\sum_{k=0}^{n-m}\binom{n-1}{k}\binom{n-1}{k+1}\binom{n-1}{k+2}\cdots\binom{n-1}{k+m-1}t^{k}
=n​Fn−1,m​(t).\displaystyle=nF_{n-1,\,m}(t). (2.7)

From the relations (2.6) and (2.7), we obtain (2.5). It follows that the polynomial sequence {Fn,m​(t)}n≥m−1\{F_{n,\,m}(t)\}_{n\geq m-1} is a Sturm sequence and so is {Hn[m]​(1,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(1,t)\}_{n\geq 1} for m≥2m\geq 2. ∎

3 Asymptotic rr-log-convexity of the Baxter numbers

In this section, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.3 by Hou and Zhang’s method on asymptotic analysis. Let us begin with a brief overview of their technique [16].

The asymptotic expansions of PP-recursive sequences were given by Birkhoff and Trjitzinsky [2] and later developed by Wimp and Zeilberger [29]. Based on their results, Hou and Zhang [16] further established a symbolic method to determine whether a PP-recursive sequence is (asymptotically) rr-log-convex.

Let {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} be a sequence of real numbers. Suppose that there exist real coefficients ℓ0,ℓ1,…,ℓm\ell_{0},\,\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m} and real exponents α0<α1<⋯<αm\alpha_{0}<\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{m} such that

limn→∞nαm​(an−∑i=0mℓinαi)=0.\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}n^{\alpha_{m}}\left(a_{n}-\sum_{i=0}^{m}\frac{\ell_{i}}{n^{\alpha_{i}}}\right)=0.

Then a Puiseux-type approximation of ana_{n}, denoted by an≈bna_{n}\approx b_{n}, is defined by the summation

bn=∑i=0mℓinαi.\displaystyle b_{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\frac{\ell_{i}}{n^{\alpha_{i}}}.

Thus, the asymptotic expansion of ana_{n} can be written in the standard little-o notation as

an=ℓ0nα0+ℓ1nα1+⋯+o⁡(1nαm).\displaystyle a_{n}=\frac{\ell_{0}}{n^{\alpha_{0}}}+\frac{\ell_{1}}{n^{\alpha_{1}}}+\cdots+o\left(\frac{1}{n^{\alpha_{m}}}\right).

Define an operator ℛ\mathscr{R} on {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} as ℛ⁡(an)=an+1/an\mathscr{R}(a_{n})=a_{n+1}/a_{n}. Clearly, ℛ2​(an)=an​an+2/an+12\mathscr{R}^{2}(a_{n})=a_{n}a_{n+2}/a_{n+1}^{2}. Hou and Zhang [16] derived the following criterion for asymptotic rr-log-convexity.

Theorem 3.1 ([16, Theorem 2.2]).

Let {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} be a positive sequence such that the ratio ℛ2​(an)\mathscr{R}^{2}(a_{n}) has a Puiseux-type approximation of the form

ℛ2​(an)=1+cnα+⋯+o⁡(1nβ),\displaystyle\mathscr{R}^{2}(a_{n})=1+\frac{c}{n^{\alpha}}+\cdots+o\left(\frac{1}{n^{\beta}}\right), (3.1)

where 0<α≤β0<\alpha\leq\beta. If c>0c>0 and α≥2\alpha\geq 2, then {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is asymptotically (⌊β−α2⌋+1)\left(\lfloor\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}\rfloor+1\right)-log-convex.

This reduces the proof of the asymptotic result in Theorem 1.3 to finding a Puiseux-type approximation of ℛ2​(Bn)\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n}) that satisfies (3.1) with c>0c>0 and α≥2\alpha\geq 2 for any given integer β≥2\beta\geq 2. In fact, there exists a systematic theory for handling problems of this type associated with PP-recursive sequences. Recall that a sequence {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is said to be PP-recursive of order jj if it satisfies a recurrence relation of the form

an+j=R0​(n)​an+R1​(n)​an+1+⋯+Rj−1​(n)​an+j−1\displaystyle a_{n+j}=R_{0}(n)a_{n}+R_{1}(n)a_{n+1}+\cdots+R_{j-1}(n)a_{n+j-1} (3.2)

where each Ri​(n)R_{i}(n) is a rational function of nn, see Stanley [26, Section 6.4]. Suppose that the sequence {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} is PP-recursive, then ana_{n} can be asymptotically expressed as a finite linear combination of terms of the form

eQ⁡(ρ,n)​s​(ρ,n),\displaystyle e^{Q(\rho,n)}\,s(\rho,n),

where

Q⁡(ρ,n)\displaystyle Q(\rho,n) =μ0​n​log⁡n+∑j=1ρμj​nj/ρ,\displaystyle=\mu_{0}n\log n+\sum_{j=1}^{\rho}\mu_{j}n^{j/\rho},
s⁡(ρ,n)\displaystyle s(\rho,n) =nν∑j=0δ−1(logn)j∑k=0Kλk,jn−k/ρ,\displaystyle=n^{\nu}\sum_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(\log n)^{j}\sum_{k=0}^{K}\lambda_{k,\,j}n^{-k/\rho},

with ρ,δ,K\rho,\,\delta,\,K being positive integers and μj,ν,λk,j\mu_{j},\,\nu,\,\lambda_{k,\,j} being complex numbers. See Birkhoff and Trjitzinsky [2], Wimp and Zeilberger [29] for more details.

Furthermore, Hou and Zhang [16] also gave a symbolic method for finding an explicit NrN_{r} such that {an}n≥Nr\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq N_{r}} is rr-log-convex, when it is asymptotically log-convex. They implemented their algorithms in a Mathematica package P-rec.m, and the related command is

𝚛𝙻𝚘𝚐𝙱𝚘𝚞𝚗𝚍⁡[𝙻,𝚗,𝙽,𝚒𝚗𝚒​_​𝚟𝚊𝚕,𝚛,η]\displaystyle{\tt rLogBound[L,\ n,\ N,\ ini\_val,\ r,\ \eta]} (3.3)

where

L=(R0​(n)+R1​(n)​𝙽+⋯+Rj−1​(n)​𝙽j−1)−𝙽jL=\left(R_{0}(n)+R_{1}(n){\tt N}+\cdots+R_{j-1}(n){\tt N}^{j-1}\right)-{\tt N}^{j}

corresponds to the recurrence (3.2), 𝙽{\tt N} is the shift operator such that 𝙽⁡(an)=an+1{\tt N}(a_{n})=a_{n+1}, ini_val is a list of initial values of {an}n≥0\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}, and η\eta is the number of terms in a Puiseux-type approximation expansion of ℛ⁡(an)\mathscr{R}(a_{n}). As mentioned by Hou and Zhang [16], when η\eta is large enough, we shall get a symbolic proof of the rr-log-convexity of a given sequence.

We are now in a position to prove Theorem 1.3, following the approaches applied in [16, Corollary 3.2 and Theorem 4.2].

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

To begin with, we observe that the sequence {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is PP-recursive, satisfying the recurrence relation

(n+4)​(n+5)​Bn+2=(7​n2+35​n+40)​Bn+1+8​n​(n+1)​Bn,\displaystyle(n+4)(n+5)B_{n+2}=(7n^{2}+35n+40)B_{n+1}+8n(n+1)B_{n}, (3.4)

as recorded by Richard L. Ollerton in the OEIS [25, A001181]. Since BnB_{n} can be written as a sum of hypergeometric terms Dn,kD_{n,\,k} over kk, it is easy to verify (3.4) using Zeilberger’s algorithm [30].

Then we can apply Theorem 3.1 to prove the asymptotic rr-log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}. Clearly, Bn>0B_{n}>0 for all n≥1n\geq 1. We find a Puiseux-type approximation of BnB_{n} from the recurrence relation (3.4) by using P-rec.m11 1 See https://faculty.tju.edu.cn/146004/zh_CN/lwcg/29931/content/37248.htm#lwcgl. given by Hou [16]. For more alternative packages, see AsyRec22 2 See https://sites.math.rutgers.edu/~zeilberg/mamarim/mamarimhtml/asy.html. given by Zeilberger [31], and Asymptotics.m33 3 See http://www.kauers.de/software.html. given by Kauers [17]. First let

𝙻=(𝚗+𝟺)​(𝚗+𝟻)​𝙽𝟸−(𝟽​𝚗𝟸+𝟹𝟻​𝚗+𝟺𝟶)​𝙽−𝟾​𝚗​(𝚗+𝟷).\displaystyle{\tt L=(n+4)(n+5)N^{2}-(7n^{2}+35n+40)N-8n(n+1)}.

By running the command

𝙰𝚜𝚢⁡[𝙻,𝚗,𝙽,𝙺]\displaystyle{\tt Asy[L,\ n,\ N,\ K]} (3.5)

for K=2K=2, we find out an asymptotic expansion of BnB_{n}:

Bn=C⋅8n​n−4​(1−223​n+95527​n2+o⁡(1n2)),\displaystyle B_{n}=C\cdot 8^{n}n^{-4}\left(1-\frac{22}{3n}+\frac{955}{27n^{2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\right), (3.6)

where CC is a constant. In fact, C=25/(3​π)C={2^{5}}/{(\sqrt{3}\pi)}, see [7, Eq. 20]. Therefore, ℛ2​(Bn)\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n}) has the form

ℛ2​(Bn)=Bn​Bn+2Bn+12=1+4n2+o⁡(1n2).\displaystyle\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n})=\frac{B_{n}B_{n+2}}{B_{n+1}^{2}}=1+\frac{4}{n^{2}}+o\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right). (3.7)

Comparing (3.7) with (3.1), it is clear that c=4>0c=4>0, α=2>0\alpha=2>0, β=2≥α\beta=2\geq\alpha, and hence ℛ2​(Bn)\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n}) has a Puiseux-type approximation of the form (3.1). This implies that {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is asymptotically 11-log-convex by Theorem 3.1. For any r≥2r\geq 2, taking KK to be 2​r2r in the command (3.5), one can obtain a Puiseux-type approximation of BnB_{n} in the form of (3.1) with the same α\alpha and cc as those in (3.6). This leads to an asymptotic expansion of ℛ2​(Bn)\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n}) as

ℛ2​(Bn)=Bn​Bn+2Bn+12=1+4n2+⋯+o⁡(1n2​r).\displaystyle\mathscr{R}^{2}(B_{n})=\frac{B_{n}B_{n+2}}{B_{n+1}^{2}}=1+\frac{4}{n^{2}}+\cdots+o\left(\frac{1}{n^{2r}}\right).

As a result, we finally obtain the asymptotic rr-log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} by Theorem 3.1 for any positive integer rr.

For the 22-log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}, the symbolic proof is almost one-line by running the command given in (3.3). The command

𝚛𝙻𝚘𝚐𝙱𝚘𝚞𝚗𝚍⁡[𝙻,𝚗,𝙽,{𝟷, 2, 6, 22, 92}, 2, 5]\displaystyle{\tt rLogBound[L,\ n,\ N,\ \{1,\ 2,\ 6,\ 22,\ 92\},\ 2,\ 5]}

outputs {True, 13069}, which means that {Bn}n≥13069\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 13069} is 22-log-convex. Since the log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} has been proved by Došlić and Veljan [11, Theorem 4.18], it remains to check the first 13,06913,069 values of ℛ2​ℒ​(Bn)\mathscr{R}^{2}\mathscr{L}(B_{n}). We have verified that these initial values are all greater than one with Mathemtaica. It follows that {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is 22-log-convex. ∎

With the aid of the package P-rec.m, it is easy to get that {Bn}n≥882712\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 882712} is 33-log-convex. We do not prove the 33-log-convexity of {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} due to limitations of our equipment.

4 Conclusion

To conclude this paper, we present three conjectures concerning the (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sums Hn[m]​(q,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(q,t) and the Baxter numbers BnB_{n}.

In his PhD thesis, Dilks [9] studied the specialization of Hn[m]​(q,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(q,t) to m=1,2,3m=1,2,3 and presented their explicit expressions. For m=1m=1, the (q,t)(q,t)-Hoggatt sum is

Hn[1](q,t)=∑k=0n−1q(k+12)[n−1k]qtk=(1+tq)(1+tq2)⋯(1+tqn−1),H_{n}^{[1]}(q,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}q^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n-1}{k}_{q}t^{k}=(1+tq)(1+tq^{2})\cdots(1+tq^{n-1}),

and it is clear that {Hn[1]​(q,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[1]}(q,t)\}_{n\geq 1} is a generalized Sturm sequence for any fixed positive integer qq. For m≥2m\geq 2, Theorem 1.2 states that when q=1q=1, the polynomials Hn[m]​(q,t)H_{n}^{[m]}(q,t) form a Sturm sequence. In fact, we observe that this property extends to any positive integer qq for m=2,3m=2,3. This leads to the following conjecture which we have verified for 1≤q≤101\leq q\leq 10 and 1≤n≤151\leq n\leq 15 by Mathematica.

Conjecture 4.1.

For any integer q>0q>0 and m=2,3m=2,3, the polynomial sequence {Hn[m]​(q,t)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(q,t)\}_{n\geq 1} forms a Sturm sequence.

For Baxter numbers, Theorem 1.3 suggests the following conjecture.

Conjecture 4.2.

The sequence of Baxter numbers {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} is infinitely log-convex.

It is known that a Stieltjes moment sequence is infinitely log-convex [28]. However, we observe that the sequence {Bn}n≥1\{B_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} fails to be a Stieltjes moment sequence, since the fifth-order leading principal minor of its Hankel matrix is negative.

Note that the Baxter numbers can be treated as the specialization of the classical Hoggatt sums Hn[m]​(1,1)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,1) at m=3m=3. Therefore, we propose a more general conjecture as follows.

Conjecture 4.3.

The sequence of (1,1)(1,1)-Hoggatt sums {Hn[m]​(1,1)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[m]}(1,1)\}_{n\geq 1} is infinitely log-convex for any fixed m≥2m\geq 2.

The conjecture holds for m=2m=2 since the numbers Hn[2]​(1,1)H_{n}^{[2]}(1,1) are the Catalan numbers. This sequence is known to be a Stieltjes moment sequence and hence is infinitely log-convex [19]. For any fixed m≥4m\geq 4, one may adapt a similar method used in the proof of Theorem 1.3 to obtain the asymptotic rr-log-convexity of Hn[m]​(1,1)H_{n}^{[m]}(1,1). However, we have not found a unified approach that works for arbitrary mm. Applying the package P-rec.m, one can obtain that {Hn[4]​(1,1)}n≥9632\{H_{n}^{[4]}(1,1)\}_{n\geq 9632} is log-convex and {Hn[4]​(1,1)}n≥404602\{H_{n}^{[4]}(1,1)\}_{n\geq 404602} is 22-log-convex. We have verified that all initial 9,6329,632 values of ℛ2​(Hn[4]​(1,1))\mathscr{R}^{2}(H_{n}^{[4]}(1,1)) exceed one. Thus, {Hn[4]​(1,1)}n≥1\{H_{n}^{[4]}(1,1)\}_{n\geq 1} is log-convex. We do not check the initial 404,602404,602 values of ℛ2​ℒ​(Hn[4]​(1,1))\mathscr{R}^{2}\mathscr{L}(H_{n}^{[4]}(1,1)) because the limitations of our computers. All of the above results suggest that Conjecture 4.3 is probably valid.
